name: EBCI Black Walnut Pound Cake
region: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians / Indigenous Americas
imageAlt: Shelled black walnut meats, the defining ingredient in this EBCI-published pound cake
imageCredit: Photo: Ll1324, Wikimedia Commons, CC0. Ingredient image; not a photograph of the finished cake.
summary: A black walnut pound cake adapted from Lucille Wolfe and published by the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods program.
lead: A rich sour-cream pound cake carrying the unmistakable deep flavor of black walnuts, from a recipe shared by EBCI Tribal Foods.
about: The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Food Distribution Program publishes this Black Walnut Pound Cake as a community recipe adapted from Lucille Wolfe. It is a modern pound cake formula—flour, butter, shortening, eggs, sour cream and sugar—with black walnuts as the defining regional ingredient. This page keeps that modern community framing instead of inventing a pre-contact origin for a European-style cake.
story: Black walnut trees are native to eastern North America and their intensely flavored nuts have long been gathered across the southern Appalachians. The specific cake here, however, is a contemporary EBCI community recipe. Tribal Foods publishes it as part of a broad recipe collection serving present-day Cherokee households, demonstrating that living Indigenous foodways include both long-standing ingredients and newer kitchen forms.
caveat: This is an adaptation of a modern community recipe published by the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, not a ceremonial or ancient Cherokee dish. The EBCI source credits Lucille Wolfe.
prepNotes: Use black walnuts, not English walnuts
Black walnuts have a much stronger, earthier flavor and are the defining ingredient.
Coat nuts with flour
Tossing the nuts with the dry ingredients helps distribute them instead of letting them sink.
Judge by the center
Bundt pans vary; bake until a tester from the deepest part comes out with moist crumbs but no wet batter.
steps: Heat oven to 325°F. Grease and flour a 10- to 12-cup Bundt pan thoroughly.
Whisk flour and baking powder, then toss the black walnuts through the flour until coated.
Beat sugar, butter and shortening until pale and creamy, 3–4 minutes.
Whisk eggs, milk and sour cream in a separate bowl until smooth.
Add the dry mixture to the creamed fat in three additions, alternating with the wet mixture. Mix only until each addition disappears.
Fold gently once or twice to make sure the nuts are evenly distributed, then scrape batter into the pan and level the top.
Bake 75–90 minutes. Checkpoint: the cake should pull slightly from the pan edges and a tester inserted deep in the center should come out clean or with a few moist crumbs.
Cool in the pan 15 minutes, invert onto a rack and cool completely before slicing.
sources: Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods — Black Walnut Pound Cake
Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians Tribal Foods — Cherokee Foodways

name: Ethiopian Tikil Gomen
imageAlt: Ethiopian platter including tikil gomen with cabbage, potatoes and carrots
imageCredit: Photo: stu_spivack, Wikimedia Commons/Flickr, CC BY-SA 2.0. Tikil gomen appears as part of the shared platter.
summary: Ethiopian cabbage, carrots and potatoes gently cooked with onion, garlic, ginger and turmeric until tender but still distinct.
lead: Cabbage, carrot and potato turn golden with turmeric in a mild Ethiopian vegetable dish designed to balance hotter wots.
about: Tikil gomen is an Ethiopian cabbage preparation commonly cooked with carrots and potatoes. Unlike berbere-heavy wots, it is usually mild, with turmeric giving the vegetables a warm yellow color and onion, garlic and ginger supplying depth. The finished vegetables should be thoroughly tender without dissolving into mash.
story: Tikil gomen belongs naturally on Ethiopian vegetarian and fasting platters, where mild vegetables help balance lentil and chickpea dishes with more chile or spice. Published Ethiopian and Ethiopian-diaspora versions vary in the use of cumin, ginger, jalapeño and korarima. This adaptation keeps the ingredient list restrained and the texture of each vegetable recognizable.
caveat: Household versions differ in spice and vegetable ratios. This is a practical cabbage-carrot-potato form, not a single universal Ethiopian formula.
prepNotes: Cut vegetables consistently
Even pieces let potatoes and carrots finish close to the same time.
Add cabbage after firmer vegetables
Cabbage softens faster than potato and should not spend the full cook time in the pot.
Keep liquid modest
The vegetables should steam and braise in their own juices, not swim in broth.
ingredients: 3 medium waxy potatoes, cut into 3/4-inch cubes
1 small green cabbage, cored and cut into 1-inch pieces
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Heat oil in a wide covered pot over medium heat. Add onion and cook 6–8 minutes until soft and lightly golden.
Add garlic, ginger and turmeric and stir 30 seconds until fragrant.
Add carrots and potatoes, toss in the seasoned oil and cook 4 minutes.
Add water and salt, cover and reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 10 minutes.
Add cabbage and jalapeño if using, folding gently so the cabbage contacts the hot pot. Cover again and cook 12–15 minutes.
Checkpoint: potatoes should be tender when pierced, carrots should retain a little structure and cabbage should be soft without turning to puree.
Uncover and cook 2–3 minutes if free liquid remains. Taste for salt and serve warm with injera and other Ethiopian dishes.
sources: Eater — Ye Tikil Gomen Alicha from Beejhy Barhany’s Gursha

name: Senegalese Chicken Yassa
imageAlt: Typical Senegalese chicken yassa with onion sauce and rice
imageCredit: Photo: Kinesira, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Senegalese chicken yassa marinated in lemon and onion, browned, then braised beneath a deeply softened onion-mustard sauce.
lead: Chicken spends hours with lemon and onions before meeting the grill or broiler, then returns to a mountain of soft, sharp onions.
about: Chicken yassa is a Senegalese dish strongly associated with Casamance and built around an unusually large quantity of onions, citrus and chile. The chicken is marinated, browned separately and then finished in the softened onion marinade. Mustard appears in many contemporary versions, though simpler formulas may focus almost entirely on lemon, onion and oil.
story: Food historian Jessica B. Harris has written about first tasting chicken yassa in Senegal and describes the contrast of lemon, chile, onion and chicken as foundational to the dish. The browned chicken and long-cooked onions create a flavor much deeper than the short ingredient list suggests. Recipes vary enough that even Senegalese cooks disagree about olives, carrots, mustard and sweetness.
caveat: Yassa varies by household and region. This version uses mustard and olives as documented additions while keeping lemon and onions dominant.
prepNotes: Marinate at least two hours
The onions and citrus season the chicken and generate the sauce base.
Brown chicken outside the onion sauce
Broiling or grilling adds roasted flavor before the pieces return to the braise.
Give onions time
The sauce should be mostly softened onion, not a watery lemon broth.
ingredients: 1 whole chicken, about 3 1/2 lb, cut into 8 pieces
1/4 cup peanut or neutral oil, divided
1 habanero, minced or left whole for less heat
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Combine chicken, lemon juice, onions, 3 tablespoons oil, chile, salt and pepper. Refrigerate at least 2 hours, turning once.
Remove chicken and shake off onions, reserving all marinade. Broil or grill the pieces until browned on both sides; they do not need to be cooked through yet.
Heat remaining oil in a Dutch oven. Add the marinated onions with as little liquid as possible and cook over medium-low heat 20–25 minutes until very soft.
Add reserved marinade, mustard and water or stock and bring to a simmer.
Nestle in the browned chicken and olives if using. Cover partially and simmer 20–25 minutes.
Checkpoint: chicken must reach at least 165°F at the thickest part and onions should have collapsed into a glossy, intensely savory sauce.
Taste for salt and lemon balance and serve hot over white rice.
sources: Food Network — Senegalese Chicken Yassa by Jessica B. Harris
The Washington Post — Senegalese Chicken Yassa by Jessica B. Harris

name: Trinidad Chicken Pelau
imageAlt: Chicken pelau from Trinidad and Tobago
imageCredit: Photo: Grueslayer / Baldur Brückner, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Trinidad chicken pelau with caramel-browned chicken, rice, pigeon peas, coconut milk, pumpkin and green seasoning cooked in one pot.
lead: Brown sugar becomes nearly black caramel before chicken hits the pot—the signature first move in Trinidad pelau.
about: Pelau is a Trinidad and Tobago one-pot rice dish in which seasoned chicken is browned in deeply caramelized sugar before rice, pigeon peas, coconut milk and vegetables cook together. The browned sugar contributes color and a bittersweet depth; the finished dish should not taste sugary.
story: Tourism Trinidad lists pelau among the traditional foods that express the island’s layered culinary heritage. Foodie Nation’s Trinidad method emphasizes the crucial browning stage, where sugar reaches a dark amber ‘black jack’ color before seasoned chicken is added. Rice then parches briefly with the chicken before pigeon peas, aromatics, coconut and vegetables complete the pot.
caveat: Pelau varies in meat, peas, vegetables and moisture. This chicken version follows a common Trinidad structure and keeps the final rice moist but not wet.
prepNotes: Watch the sugar continuously
Caramel goes from deep brown to burnt very quickly; have seasoned chicken ready before you start.
Use a heavy pot
Even heat gives you more control over browning and reduces scorching during the rice stage.
Finish by texture
Pelau can be drier or wetter by household; stop when rice is tender and the pot is cohesive, not soupy.
ingredients: 2 lb chicken thighs and drumsticks, cut into pieces and seasoned with green seasoning
4 pimento peppers or 1 small sweet pepper, chopped
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Heat oil in a heavy pot over medium-high heat. Add brown sugar in an even layer and watch until it melts, bubbles and reaches very dark amber.
Immediately add seasoned chicken and turn vigorously to coat in caramel. Brown 8–10 minutes.
Add rice and stir 3–4 minutes so grains toast lightly in the chicken and caramel.
Add pigeon peas, garlic, onion, pimento pepper and pumpkin. Stir well.
Add coconut milk and enough water or stock to sit just above the rice. Add whole Scotch bonnet and salt.
Cover and simmer over low heat 20 minutes, then add carrot and stir once.
Continue covered or partially covered until rice is tender, adding small amounts of hot water only if needed.

Checkpoint: grains should be cooked through, chicken tender and the pot moist enough to hold together without free liquid pooling. Fold in culantro, remove whole chile and rest 10 minutes before serving.
sources: Visit Trinidad — Cuisine and traditional pelau context
Foodie Nation — Trini Chicken Pelau method
Fringe Table — Caribbean & Lowcountry food guide

name: Azerbaijani Meat Qutab
imageCredit: Photo: Interfase, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Paper-thin Azerbaijani qutab folded over seasoned lamb or beef, cooked on a hot dry pan and served with sumac, yogurt and pomegranate.
lead: A thin unleavened dough folds around just enough meat to cook through on a blistering-hot saj or skillet.
about: Qutab is a widespread Azerbaijani folded flatbread or pastry cooked on a hot saj. Fillings include meat, herbs, pumpkin and offal. Meat qutab uses a very thin layer of minced lamb or beef with onion so the filling cooks in the short time needed to blister the dough.
story: Azerbaijan’s official tourism site describes qutab as a portable street snack whose name is connected with the Azerbaijani verb for folding. Meat versions are commonly served with sumac or qatıq yogurt, and pomegranate can appear inside or alongside. The extreme thinness of both wrapper and filling is what makes the quick dry-pan cooking possible.
caveat: Regional qutab fillings and serving styles differ. This page follows Azerbaijan.travel’s published meat version rather than treating qutab as one fixed recipe.
prepNotes: Roll almost paper-thin
Thick dough will stay chewy before the meat finishes.
Spread meat thinly
A dense mound cannot cook safely in the short griddle time.
Use a very hot dry pan
Traditional saj cooking is fast and relatively dry; a cast-iron skillet is the home substitute.
ingredients: 1 small onion, grated and squeezed lightly
Ground sumac and plain yogurt, for serving
steps: Mix flour and salt, then add water gradually and knead 6–8 minutes until smooth and firm. Cover and rest 30 minutes.
Mix meat with grated onion, pepper and filling salt.
Divide dough into 8 balls and roll each into a thin 8-inch circle, using flour sparingly.
Spread a very thin layer of meat across one half, leaving a narrow clean border. Add a few pomegranate seeds if using.
Fold the empty half over the filling and press the curved edge tightly closed, pushing out trapped air.
Cook on a very hot dry cast-iron skillet or griddle 2–3 minutes per side.
Checkpoint: dough should show dark toasted spots and filling should be fully cooked with no raw center. If qutab browns before meat cooks, the filling is too thick.
Brush lightly with butter and serve immediately with sumac and yogurt.
sources: Fringe Table — Caucasus, Central & West Asia food guide

name: Bhutanese Kewa Datshi
imageAlt: Bhutanese kewa datshi potato and cheese dish
imageCredit: Photo: Rigzen Dema, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
summary: Bhutanese kewa datshi: sliced potatoes, onion, tomato and green chile simmered under a melted cheese sauce and served with rice.
lead: Potatoes and cheese make the gentler cousin of ema datshi, still unmistakably Bhutanese in its chile-and-datshi logic.
about: Kewa datshi means potato and cheese. It belongs to Bhutan’s datshi family of dishes, where local cheese forms a sauce around vegetables or chile. Compared with ema datshi, potatoes make this version milder and more substantial, though green chile is still a normal part of the pot.
story: Bhutan’s Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources eCookbook identifies kewa datshi as one of the country’s famous dishes and publishes a straightforward potato, onion, tomato, green chile and cheese method. Bhutan tourism resources similarly describe it as a popular, nourishing specialty and a milder relative of ema datshi. Imported cheese substitutions change the flavor, but the simmer-then-melt method remains accessible to home cooks.
caveat: Traditional datshi cheese is difficult to source outside Bhutan. A mix of farmer cheese, feta and mild melting cheese can approximate its tang and body but is still a substitute.
prepNotes: Slice potatoes evenly
Thin uniform pieces cook before the cheese is added.
Do not brown the onions
The official-style method is closer to simmering than sautéing deeply.
Let cheese melt before stirring hard
Gentle heat keeps the sauce cohesive.
ingredients: 1 1/2 lb waxy potatoes, peeled and sliced 1/4 inch thick
6 oz farmer cheese, feta or a blend with mild melting cheese
1 tsp kosher salt, plus more to taste
steps: Combine potatoes, onion, tomato, chiles, oil and enough water to almost cover the potatoes in a wide saucepan.
Bring to a boil, cover and cook over medium-high heat 10–12 minutes.
Checkpoint: potatoes should be nearly tender but still hold their slices.
Scatter cheese over the pot, reduce heat and cover again for 3–5 minutes until melted.
Gently fold the cheese through the cooking liquid rather than stirring aggressively.
Simmer uncovered another 2–4 minutes until the sauce lightly coats the potatoes.
Taste for salt, rest 2 minutes and serve hot with Bhutanese red rice or steamed white rice.
sources: Fringe Table — Himalayas & South Asia food guide

name: Malaysian Nasi Lemak
imageAlt: Malaysian nasi lemak with coconut rice, sambal, egg, anchovies, peanuts and cucumber
imageCredit: Photo: Hajar Aznam, Wikimedia Commons, Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike licensed
summary: Malaysian nasi lemak with fragrant coconut-pandan rice, sambal, crisp anchovies, peanuts, egg and cucumber.
lead: Coconut rice scented with pandan sits at the center, surrounded by sambal, anchovies, peanuts, egg and cool cucumber.
about: Nasi lemak is a quintessential Malaysian rice meal built around rice cooked in coconut milk and pandan. The classic plate or banana-leaf packet pairs that fragrant rice with sambal, fried anchovies, peanuts, egg and cucumber; larger versions may add fried chicken, fish, squid or rendang.
story: Tourism Malaysia repeatedly identifies nasi lemak as a defining Malaysian dish and a beloved breakfast across communities. Its name points to the richness of coconut-enriched rice, but the meal depends on contrasts around it: hot sambal, salty-crisp ikan bilis, crunchy peanuts, rich egg and fresh cucumber. It ranges from inexpensive wrapped breakfast portions to elaborate restaurant plates.
caveat: Sambal formulas and accompaniments vary widely. This version focuses on the classic coconut rice and core garnishes and uses a straightforward dried-chile sambal.
prepNotes: Rinse rice gently
Remove loose starch but avoid rough handling that breaks jasmine grains.
Knot pandan leaves
A knot bruises the leaf and helps release aroma while keeping it easy to remove.
Cook sambal until the oil separates
The chile-onion paste should lose its raw edge and become dark, glossy and slightly sweet.
ingredients: 3 cups jasmine rice, rinsed and drained
12 dried red chiles, soaked and drained
2 tbsp tamarind concentrate diluted with 1/4 cup water
1 cup small dried anchovies, fried crisp
steps: Combine rice, coconut milk, water, pandan, lemongrass and salt. Bring to a gentle boil, cover tightly and cook over very low heat 15 minutes. Rest covered 10 minutes before fluffing.
Blend soaked chiles, shallots, garlic and shrimp paste if using into a coarse sambal paste with a splash of water.
Heat oil over medium-low heat and cook sambal 12–18 minutes, stirring often.
Checkpoint: the paste should darken substantially, lose its raw-onion aroma and show small beads of oil around the edges.
Add tamarind water and sugar and simmer 5 minutes. Adjust salt and sweetness so the sambal is hot, tangy and savory with a gentle sweet edge.
Arrange coconut rice with sambal, fried anchovies, peanuts, egg and cucumber. Add optional chicken, fish or rendang as a larger meal.
sources: Tourism Malaysia — Nasi Lemak recipe by Juliah Rais-Morres
Tourism Malaysia — Malaysian Food: Nasi Lemak
Fringe Table — Southeast Asia food guide
